findings.title: Local cache is populated before the store call, so the device limit is bypassed after the first rejection
findings.body: In `tagDeviceUI` the cache entry is written (`a.localCache.SetDefault(key, struct{}{})`) before `a.anonStore.CreateOrUpdateDevice` is invoked. With the new limit logic, the first request from an over-limit device returns `ErrDeviceLimitReached` and is denied, but the cache key is already set, so every subsequent request from that same device for the cache TTL (29 min) short-circuits with `return nil` and is authenticated without ever consulting the limit. The result is that the configured `device_limit` is enforced only on the very first request per device per cache window, i.e. effectively not enforced, and users see a confusing "fails once then works" behaviour. The cache should only be populated after a successful store call (or the failed key removed on error).

findings.title: rowsAffected == 0 wrongly reported as ErrDeviceLimitReached for existing devices on MySQL
findings.body: `updateDevice` maps `rowsAffected == 0` to `ErrDeviceLimitReached`. On MySQL, `RowsAffected()` reports *changed* rows, not matched rows (unless CLIENT_FOUND_ROWS is set), so an UPDATE that matches an already-tracked device but writes identical column values (same client_ip/user_agent and an `updated_at` that truncates to the same second — MySQL DATETIME has second precision here) returns 0. In that case an existing, already-counted device is denied access with "device limit reached" even though it is within the limit. Additionally, this error value conflates two distinct conditions ("device not found/expired" vs "limit reached"), which makes the surfaced error misleading; the device-not-found case should be distinguished or detected via a SELECT/matched-rows check.

findings.title: Check-then-insert on device count is racy and can exceed the configured limit
findings.body: `CreateOrUpdateDevice` performs `CountDevices` and then, in a separate session, an INSERT ... ON CONFLICT. Concurrent anonymous requests for new device IDs can all read a count below `deviceLimit` and then all insert, so the stored device count can exceed the configured limit by the number of concurrent requests. Since the limit is a licensing/abuse control, this is an enforcement hole. Consider doing the count and insert inside one transaction, or enforcing the limit with a conditional INSERT (e.g. `INSERT ... SELECT ... WHERE (SELECT COUNT(*) ...) < limit`) so the check and write are atomic.

findings.title: Device tagging moved into the synchronous auth path, adding DB round-trips to every anonymous request
findings.body: `TagDevice` was previously executed in a background goroutine with its own timeout; it is now called synchronously inside `Authenticate`. Every anonymous request whose device ID is not in the 29-minute local cache now blocks on a `SELECT COUNT(*) FROM anon_device` (when `device_limit > 0`) plus an INSERT/UPDATE before authentication completes. For instances with high anonymous traffic and many distinct device IDs this adds DB load and request latency on the hot login path, and a slow/locked DB now stalls (rather than merely fails to record) anonymous requests. If synchronous behaviour is required only to enforce the limit, consider only doing the blocking path when a limit is configured, and/or caching the device count.

findings.title: ErrDeviceLimitReached is a plain error, so clients get an opaque 500 instead of an actionable status
findings.body: `ErrDeviceLimitReached` is created with `fmt.Errorf`, and `client.go` returns it directly from `Authenticate`. Because it carries no `errutil` status/public message, the authn broker will surface it as a generic internal error (HTTP 500 with no meaningful message) to the browser, so an operator-configured device limit looks like a server failure to the end user and is hard to diagnose from the response. Define it with `errutil` (e.g. a 429/403-style status with a public message) so the limit rejection is reported as an intentional, documented condition.

findings.title: New auth.anonymous device_limit option is not added to defaults.ini/sample.ini or documented
findings.body: `cfg.AnonymousDeviceLimit = anonSection.Key("device_limit").MustInt64(0)` introduces a new user-facing configuration key `[auth.anonymous] device_limit`, but the PR does not add it to `conf/defaults.ini`/`conf/sample.ini` nor to the configuration docs. Without the defaults.ini entry the option is undiscoverable (and the documented-config consistency checks Grafana runs over defaults.ini/docs will flag it), and operators have no documentation of the behaviour when the limit is hit (new devices are rejected, existing devices continue to work).

findings.title: Provider signature change (AnonStore -> db.DB) requires DI wiring updates not included in this PR
findings.body: `ProvideAnonymousDeviceService` no longer accepts an `anonstore.AnonStore` and instead takes `db.DB`, constructing the store internally, while `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` gained a second `deviceLimit int64` parameter. No changes to the wire provider sets (`pkg/server/wire.go` and the enterprise equivalents) are included. If `anonstore.ProvideAnonDBStore` / `wire.Bind(new(anonstore.AnonStore), ...)` are still listed there, wire generation will fail (no provider for `int64`, and/or an unused provider), breaking the build; conversely any other consumer that relied on injecting an `AnonStore` now loses it. The DI configuration needs to be updated in the same change.

findings.title: No test for the main intended path: updating an already-tracked device while at the limit
findings.body: `TestIntegrationBeyondDeviceLimit` only asserts that a *new* device ID is rejected once the limit is reached. The core behaviour of the feature — that an already-stored device keeps working (its client_ip/user_agent/updated_at are updated) when the count is at or above `deviceLimit` — is untested, as is the expiry window in `updateDevice` (a device older than `anonymousDeviceExpiration` should not be revived). These are exactly the paths where the `rowsAffected == 0` heuristic can misfire, so they should be covered.

findings.title: anonymousDeviceLimit initialised to undefined narrows its type to `undefined`
findings.body: `anonymousDeviceLimit = undefined;` with no type annotation makes the class property's inferred type `undefined`, so any frontend code that tries to use it numerically (e.g. `config.anonymousDeviceLimit > 0`) will be a type error even though the backend always sends a number. Note also that the Go DTO field has no `omitempty`, so the value is `0` (not absent) when the limit is disabled; annotate as `anonymousDeviceLimit: number | undefined = undefined` (or `number`) and make the frontend contract explicit about 0 meaning "no limit".
